title: Time boxing
blurb: Define time boxing: fix the time and the resources, and let the scope flex by priority.
question: A council's digital team has a fixed six-week window and a fixed team to deliver a parking-permit app before a policy change. Halfway through, it's clear not every requested feature will be ready. Using time boxing, what should change?

teach.h: Fix the time, flex the scope
teach.body: Time boxing gives the team a fixed period of time, with fixed resources, to deliver an agreed set of work. The end of the box does not move. If it becomes clear that not everything will fit, the lowest-priority work is dropped or deferred to a later box. The date holds, the team holds; the scope gives way.

Formally: a time box is a fixed period of time, with fixed resources and cost, in which to deliver an agreed set of objectives or work. Plainly: 'We have exactly this long and these people; let's deliver the most valuable things we can.' In a time box it is the scope (features or requirements) that is adjusted, not the time or the resources.

items.label: time: the end date does not move
resources and cost: same team, same budget
scope: lower priorities dropped or deferred

teach.caption: Time boxing is the classic technique of iterative approaches, where time and cost are fixed and scope flexes.
Musts are protected. Coulds are the first to go if time runs short, then Shoulds.

teach.h: Scenario: the permit app in time boxes
teach.caption: Each box has a fixed length. Whatever is delivered by the end of week 6 goes live with the policy.

teach.body: By week 3 the team sees it cannot finish everything. The Musts (apply, pay, digital permit) stay in. The Should, renewal reminders, is deferred to a later release. The Could, a dark-mode screen, is dropped. Nobody extends the deadline or borrows developers from another team. The app launches on the policy date with the features that matter most.

items: Delivery dates are predictable because the end of each box is fixed.
It forces clear prioritisation, so the most valuable work is done first.
The immovable deadline stops work expanding to fill the time.
Regular, usable deliveries give early feedback and early value.

teach.text: In a time box, the SCOPE flexes. Distractors will offer 'extend the deadline', 'add more people' or 'increase the budget'. All wrong: time and resources are the fixed elements. If asked what is fixed in an iterative, time-boxed approach, the answer is time and cost, not scope and quality.

items: Time box: a fixed period, with fixed resources and cost, to deliver an agreed set of work.
The end date doesn't move; lower-priority scope is dropped or deferred.
Prioritisation (often MoSCoW) decides what is delivered first and what can go.
Used mainly in iterative approaches, for example sprints.
Benefits: predictable dates, focus on value, work can't expand without limit.

summary: You can now define time boxing as a fixed period, with fixed resources, in which to deliver an agreed set of work, where scope (not time or resources) is adjusted by priority. You can also explain why it relies on prioritisation such as MoSCoW and why it gives predictable delivery.

A.q: Complete the statement: in a time box, it is the ______ that is adjusted if needed.
A.why: Time and resources are fixed in a time box; scope flexes by priority.

whyNot.0: The end date of a time box is fixed.
whyNot.1: The team (resources) is fixed for the time box.
whyNot.3: Cost is fixed along with time and resources.

A.q: Which of the following best defines time boxing?
options: A fixed period to deliver an agreed set of work
A buffer of time added to the critical path
A way of estimating from a similar project
A period of float shared between activities
A.why: Time boxing sets a fixed period of time (with fixed resources) to deliver an agreed set of work or objectives.

whyNot.1: A buffer added to a path is a critical chain idea, not time boxing.
whyNot.2: Estimating from a similar project is analogous estimating.
whyNot.3: Float is flexibility from the network logic, not a time box.

A.q: Which of the following are held FIXED in a time box?
A.why: A time box fixes the time and the resources (and therefore cost); the scope flexes.

whyNot.0: Scope is the element that flexes, so it isn't fixed.
whyNot.1: Time is fixed, but scope is not.
whyNot.2: Resources are fixed, but scope is not.

B.q: Halfway through a fixed six-week time box, the team sees that two 'could have' features won't be finished. What should happen?
options: Extend the box by a week
B.why: In a time box the date and team are fixed, so the lowest-priority items are dropped or deferred.

whyNot.0: Extending the box breaks its central rule: the end date is fixed.
whyNot.2: Resources are fixed in a time box, so adding people isn't the response.
whyNot.3: Pausing would move the end date, which a time box doesn't allow.

B.q: Which prioritisation technique is commonly used to decide what is delivered within a time box?
B.why: MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't have this time) ranks requirements so the most important are delivered first.

whyNot.2: RACI shows who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
whyNot.3: Tuckman describes the stages of team development.

B.q: What does the 'W' in MoSCoW stand for?
B.why: W is 'Won't have this time': agreed as out of scope for now, possibly for a later time box.

whyNot.0: Not the term used: the agreed wording is 'won't have this time'.
whyNot.1: A wish list isn't a MoSCoW category.
whyNot.2: Not a MoSCoW category; 'could have' covers nice-to-haves.

C.q:
Which TWO are benefits of time boxing?
1. Delivery dates are predictable
2. Every requested feature is guaranteed
3. Work is prioritised by value
4. The team can grow to meet demand
C.why: Fixed end dates make delivery predictable, and fitting work into the box forces prioritisation by value.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: lower-priority features may be dropped.
whyNot.1: Both are false: scope flexes and resources are fixed.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: resources are fixed in a time box.

C.q: A product owner insists ALL features must be delivered in the current time box, even if the date moves. Why does this conflict with time boxing?
options: Time boxes fix time, not scope
Time boxes fix scope, not time
Time boxes have no end date
C.why: Time boxing fixes the time and flexes the scope; insisting on all scope at the cost of the date reverses that.

whyNot.1: This is the wrong way round: time is fixed and scope flexes.
whyNot.2: Time boxing depends heavily on clear priorities.
whyNot.3: A fixed end date is the defining feature of a time box.

C.q: Which statement about a time box is NOT correct?
options: Its end date is set in advance
Its resources are set in advance
Its work is agreed and prioritised
Its scope cannot change at all
C.why: The scope of a time box can and does flex: lower-priority work is dropped or deferred to protect the date.

whyNot.0: This is correct: the end date is fixed.
whyNot.1: This is correct: the resources are fixed.
whyNot.2: This is correct: the work is agreed and prioritised, often with MoSCoW.

reteach.title: Think of packing for a weekend with one cabin bag
reteach.question: Your flight leaves at 6 am and the airline allows exactly one small cabin bag. You've laid out far more than will fit. What gives?

blocks.body: The flight time is fixed and the bag size is fixed. So you prioritise: passport, phone charger and medication are Musts; a warm jumper is a Should; the third pair of shoes is a Could. When the bag is full, the Coulds stay at home. You don't move the flight or buy a second bag. That's a time box: the container is fixed, the contents flex.

blocks.h: What makes it into the bag

blocks.body: In a project time box, the period and team are the fixed bag. The features are the contents, packed in priority order. Whatever doesn't fit is deferred or dropped, and the delivery date holds.

whyNot.0: Float is flexibility in the network, not a time box.
whyNot.2: A milestone is a moment; a time box is a period.

test.q: Time is running short in a time box. Which response fits the technique?
options: Extend the end date by a few days
Bring in extra staff to catch up
Cut testing so that all is delivered
test.why: Scope is the element that flexes, so lower-priority work is dropped or deferred.

whyNot.0: The end date of a time box is fixed.
whyNot.1: Resources are fixed in a time box.
whyNot.3: Delivering untested work trades away quality; the technique flexes scope instead.

explain.body: Time boxes depend on clear priorities. MoSCoW sorts requirements into Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time. Musts are protected; Coulds go first.

test.q: Which MoSCoW category must be delivered for the time box to succeed?
test.why: Must-haves are the minimum needed; without them the delivery fails.

whyNot.1: Should-haves are important but can be deferred if necessary.
whyNot.2: Could-haves are the first to be dropped.
whyNot.3: Won't-haves are agreed as out of scope for now.

explain.body: A fixed end date makes delivery predictable, forces prioritisation and stops work expanding to fill the time. Time boxing is used mainly in iterative approaches, such as sprints.

test.q: How does a fixed end date help to stop work expanding?
options: It forces the team to prioritise
It adds float to every activity
It removes the need for reviews
It fixes every feature in scope
test.why: Because the date can't move, the team must choose what matters most and contain the work within the period.

whyNot.2: Reviews are a normal part of each time box.
whyNot.3: Scope flexes in a time box; it isn't fixed.
